This architect's building melted a car.
And it wasn't even his first death ray.
Las Vegas, twenty ten. A shiny new hotel opens, with a giant curved glass wall wrapped around the pool.
A guest is lying by the pool when he smells burning hair.
His plastic bag melts. Drink cups start drooping.
When he complains, the staff just giggle.
Yeah, we know. We call it the death ray.
Three years later, the same architect is finishing a skyscraper in London. Same shiny glass. Same curve.
A man parks his Jaguar on the street below.
When he comes back, the mirror is melted. The badge is melted. The panels are melted.
A reporter walks over with a frying pan, and cooks an egg on the pavement.
Wait. How does a building cook an egg?
You see, a curved glass wall works like a giant magnifying glass.
Ever burned a leaf with one as a kid? Same trick.
The curve catches sunlight from the whole building, and squeezes it onto one spot on the street. Up to fifteen times stronger than normal sunshine.
London ends up bolting giant sunshades onto the tower.
When I first came to London years ago, it wasn't like this. Now you have all these sunny days.
